newsitem.title: MEXICO: Insurers foresee big market for securitized risk.
newsitem.headline: Insurers foresee big market for securitized risk.

text.p: MEXICO CITY, July 17, Reuter - The securitization of insurance risk may only be in its infancy right now, but several insurers at a conference here this week said they expect it to play an increasingly important role in the global insurance industry in years to come.
"Securitization of risk is a market waiting to happen," Chubb Corp chief executive Dean O'Hare told the International Insurance Society conference.

"It may still have a while longer to wait, but eventually an innovator will bring together the insurance and capital markets capabilities to take this much-talked-about idea from intriguing concept to money-making reality," he said.
Risk securitization refers to the concept of transfering insurance risk to the capital markets, especially through the sale of a new breed of bonds.
A couple of such risk bond deals have been completed in the last few months, but insurers and bankers are still experimenting with this new type of security.
Just last month, USAA completed a $400 million bond offering that ties investors' returns to the company's East Coast hurricane losses.
Late last year, St. Paul Cos Inc's St. Paul Re completed a risk bond offering for nearly $70 million.

At least another three to six deals are in the pipeline for completion within the next six months, and two of them may end up larger than the USAA deal, said Gary Parr, head of Morgan Stanley's global insurance group, speaking to Reuters after his presentation at the conference on Wednesday afternoon.

But the market for these deals has been struggling to get off the ground, partly because the price of reinsurance is currently attractive, giving insurers little incentive to experiment with a new and somewhat more costly alternative.
In addition, it is taking time to educate institutional investors, the buyers of these bonds, about how they work and why they might be a good investment, the speakers said.
The bonds, which have been private placements with institutional investors, are generally designed to provide insurers with capital in case of a large catastrophe.
Reinsurance, which insurers have traditionally used for that purpose, usually becomes quite expensive following a big catastrophe.

And huge catastrophe losses over the last few years have made many insurers nervous about how they will cope with a future blockbuster catastrophe that produces insured losses on the order of $50 bllion. Hurricane Andrew generated insured losses of about $20 billion.

Although a $50-billion event would devastate the insurance industry, the $19 trillion capital markets might be able to absorb such a loss a lot more easily, ACE Ltd chief executive Brian Duperreault said in his presentation on Tuesday.

"Securitization is a very major trend," CNA Financial Corp chief executive Dennis Chookaszian said in his presentation at the conference on Monday. But he also said such a market may take as long as 10 to 15 years to fully develop -- about the time that was needed to develop the mortgage-backed securities market.

Even so, risk bonds are likely to become a very attractive instrument for big global reinsurers, which have few alternatives for diversifying such large risks, Swiss Reinsurance Group RUKZ.S chief executive Walter Kielholz said in his presentation at the conference Wednesday.
Big global reinsurers like Swiss Re, he said, currently must reduce the coverage they can make available to the market because they have no other way of diversifying their risk portfolios, he said.
Swiss Re, he said, is actively working to develop such risk bonds and would use them itself to reduce its own exposure to catastrophic risks.
In addition, he said, he expects such bonds to one day become actively traded as well.
"Maybe it will never work. But, I'm very confident it will work," he told the conference. And one day, it "will become an important part of our professional lives."
